stories.headline: Another hockey team in Texas? What you need to know about NHL expansion
stories.summary: A 33rd team could begin play in the coming seasons -- with its home rink in the Lone Star State.
stories.byline: Ryan Clark and Kristen Shilton and Greg Wyshynski
stories.body:
Since June 23, the debate about where an NHL expansion team should go in Texas has been focused on two cities: Houston and Austin.

Although Houston remains the largest metropolitan area in the nation without an NHL franchise, Austin has thrived as one of the fastest-growing markets for more than 15 years.

This all started when NHL commissioner Gary Bettman said the league is exploring placing a second team in Texas with Austin and Houston as potential targets. Bettman said the NHL entered into an agreement with the Friedkin family, which had around six months to explore placing a team in either city. The family agreed to an investment of $3.5 billion that includes an expansion fee and building costs for an NHL arena.

Adding another team in Texas, where the Dallas Stars have played since 1993, would mark the third time since 2017 that the NHL has expanded its footprint. The NHL added its 31st franchise in 2017 with the Vegas Golden Knights and grew to its current 32-team dynamic in 2021 when it added the Seattle Kraken.

Now it appears that a 33rd franchise could be on the way. As are the many questions that come with a major development for the NHL at a time in which its revenue from last season was between $7.5 billion to $8 billion.

ESPN NHL reporters Ryan S. Clark, Kristen Shilton and Greg Wyshynski are here to answer those questions about Austin, Houston and what it could all mean going forward.

How did Austin get on the NHL's expansion radar?
Sometimes, the NHL expansion process is fairly straightforward. When Las Vegas was looking to land a team, it was an effort driven by billionaire Bill Foley with no other owner or ownership group seeking to buy the franchise or build an arena for one.

In other cases, there are multiple groups seeking to land a franchise. Seattle had several possibilities for both ownership and arena sites before Seattle Hockey Partners secured the Kraken and refurbished Climate Pledge Arena. In Atlanta, where the NHL is expected to expand for a third time after the Flames and Thrashers relocated to Canada, there are three different ownership groups vying to own a team as an anchor for real estate projects.

Competition can be a good thing in negotiations. The NHL's potential second franchise in Texas didn't really have any: It was the Friedkin family as the owners, and Houston was the destination. So Austin entered the picture as another option for the Friedkins.

But rather than just being a stalking horse in the expansion race, Austin started to garner more attention from the Friedkin family as a possible home for its expansion team. The demographics were hockey-friendly. There was a ton of tech money to be had. An NHL franchise in Houston would be another pro team in a crowded sports market, much like the Kraken were in Seattle -- a market that is even more competitive when the NBA is in season. An NHL team in Austin would be more like the Golden Knights were in Vegas: the first ones through the door among the "big four" sports, immediately creating a bond with local fans.

At some point in the process, Austin's momentum was such that it became the group's preferred destination. But that doesn't necessarily mean the NHL is destined for the land of hipsters. Just because an owner has the financial means to run a team doesn't mean that the league and its 32 members are going to approve where that group wants to place a franchise. -- Wyshynski

What is the pro sports footprint for Austin and Houston, and has it ever included any form of hockey?
Austin has a unique sports landscape. The University of Texas isn't a professional team, but its programs such as football, men's and women's basketball, baseball, softball, men's and women's swimming and diving along with men's and women's track and field have strong followings.

The market's first and lone professional team among the major men's leagues is Austin FC in Major League Soccer. Until Austin FC began MLS play five years ago, the city was the largest market in the nation without a pro team. Austin also has the Circuit of the Americas, a track that has hosted Formula 1 for the annual United States Grand Prix since 2012 and the Texas Grand Prix as part of the NASCAR Cup Series since 2021.

Austin has also been home to minor league teams. The Austin Spurs, the G League affiliate of the San Antonio Spurs, play in the Cedar Park suburb. The suburb of Round Rock is home to Round Rock Express, the Triple-A affiliate of the Texas Rangers. Then there are the Texas Stars, who also play in Cedar Park and are the AHL affiliate to the NHL's Dallas Stars. Austin has had the Stars since the team relocated from Iowa in 2009.

Houston has a more established professional sports scene, with six teams across the major men's and women's leagues starting in 2027. The oldest team is the Houston Astros; the two-time World Series champions have played in the city since 1962. The Houston Rockets have been around since 1967, winning two NBA championships in the 1990s. Houston initially lost its NFL team to Nashville but gained another with the Houston Texans, founded in 1999 with their first season in 2002.

The city expanded into soccer in 2006 with the Houston Dynamo joining MLS and winning consecutive titles in 2006 and 2007; the Houston Dash joined the National Women's Soccer League in 2014. Houston was also home to the Houston Comets of the WNBA until the franchise folded in 2008. The Fertitta family, which owns the Rockets, reached an agreement in March to purchase the Connecticut Sun, relocate the team to Houston and rename it the Houston Comets.

Houston has a bit of a hockey history. Minor league hockey came to the city for a few years in the late 1940s. It returned in 1972 when the WHA encountered setbacks in its attempt to have a team in Dayton, Ohio. That led to the team moving to Houston, where it became the Aeros. Led by Gordie Howe and his sons Mark and Marty, the franchise won two league titles. The Aeros' final season was in 1979, before the WHL disbanded.

The second version of the Aeros played in Houston for 19 seasons. They were initially part of the defunct IHL before joining the AHL back in 2001. The Aeros were the affiliate for the Minnesota Wild -- and the Stars for one season -- before relocating to Iowa in 2013. -- Clark

What is the Friedkin family's background?
This would be the family's first venture into owning a North American professional sports team, but it has experience as an owner in European soccer.

Dan Friedkin, who has a master's degree from Rice University in Houston, is the owner and president of AS Roma in the Italian Serie A and the owner and chairman of Everton FC in the English Premier League. He also owns AS Cannes of Ligue 3, the French third division.

Friedkin took control of Roma in August 2020, and the club has finished in the top seven of Serie A every season since. The Giallorossi captured the UEFA Conference League, the third tier of European club competition, in 2022. In 2023, they finished second in the Europa League, the second-tier European club competition. Roma finished third in Serie A in 2025-26 and are competing in the premier European club competition -- the UEFA Champions League -- this season.

He took over Everton in December 2024, and the club finished with consecutive 13th-place finishes in the 20-team Premier League. Last season, the club left its famed Goodison Park venue and moved into Hill Dickinson Stadium, the eighth-largest soccer venue in England. -- Clark

Expansion teams usually struggle to start. Is there a reason to think this one could be good right away?
Absolutely, thanks to the lessons it will have learned from the Vegas and Seattle expansion drafts. (Though the Utah Mammoth are technically an expansion team, their players were ported over from the Arizona Coyotes when that franchise ended its existence.)

It's expected that any new expansion team will have the same rules as the Golden Knights and Kraken did during their respective drafts:

NHL teams can protect either eight skaters and a goaltender or seven forwards, three defensemen and a goaltender.
Teams must expose at least two forwards and one defenseman who are under contract for the inaugural season of the expansion team. Teams must also expose one goalie who is under contract for that season or a restricted free agent.
Teams are required, with some exceptions, to protect any player with a no-movement clause.

Famously, the Golden Knights leveraged those rules into a series of significant trades with jittery teams that had a little over a year to prepare for the expansion draft. That netted Vegas players such as Shea Theodore, Alex Tuch and Reilly Smith, along with several high draft picks.

Infamously, Seattle didn't have the same opportunity, as teams better understood the rules, were more prepared and didn't flinch from expansion draft pressure points. Vegas made the Stanley Cup Final in its inaugural season and won in 2023. Seattle finished with the league's third-worst record in its first season and has yet to find its footing as a franchise: making the playoffs once in five years and failing to leverage its expansion draft class into roster upgrades.

A new Texas franchise will have the same fundamental advantages that this draft format offers. Building around the fourth-best defensemen from other teams' rosters is a good starting point. Populating the forward group with veteran depth players can build a solid foundation. The same can be said about the veteran backup goalies the draft offers up.

But immediate success for a team in Houston or Austin will come down to three factors:

1. Goaltending. Simply put, Vegas had it in Year 1 with Marc-Andre Fleury and Seattle did not have it with Philipp Grubauer and Chris Driedger, who combined to give the Kraken the worst save percentage in the NHL that season.

2. Coaching. The Golden Knights had a strong starting point with their roster, but it wasn't an All-Star team. Coach Gerard Gallant maximized the players' abilities with his system, earning instant success. Seattle's Dave Hakstol was unable to give the Kraken a discernible personality during his three years as head coach despite overseeing their only playoff appearance and series win. The right coach can get instant results.

3. Leveraging location. Austin and Houston have quality-of-life advantages that could be desirable to NHL players. But Texas as a whole has one edge that has led to on-ice success in several markets, including Dallas: no state income tax. Whether tax relief is the reason the Stars, Panthers, Lightning and Golden Knights have found tremendous success in the past decade, it'll be an advantage as well for the new Texas team. -- Wyshynski

How would a 33-team NHL compare with other major pro leagues in North America? And if the NHL wants an even number, what other markets will it consider?
If the NHL does add a 33rd team, it stands to be the largest major professional sports league by club count (the NFL has 32 teams, while the NBA, MLB and MLS clock in with 30). There have been ongoing talks in other leagues -- namely MLB and the NBA -- about potential expansion in the near future as well. But those leagues, like the NHL, want to be prudent about creating another mouth to feed. Diluting an already good, established product is of paramount concern with any expansion proposition. How many star players are available who could make a new franchise instantly exciting?

Granted, there's a considerable pipeline of players in the current landscape -- from the junior ranks through college and European clubs -- so adding another 20 or more to a new franchise isn't necessarily a huge lift. It's just about finding the right ones, which is the goal of any team.

When it comes to having an odd number of NHL teams, commissioner Gary Bettman has said in the past that he's not concerned about the divisions being somewhat off-kilter.

"Symmetry, I don't think, should necessarily govern expansion," Bettman said in June. "You expand if you think it makes sense and enhances what the league has."

So it's not imperative that the NHL have a second potential landing spot in mind. However, Atlanta and Phoenix will likely continue to be discussed as possible destinations for a future franchise. Among the main factors in those discussions is existing infrastructure: What sort of arena space is already there, or how long would it take to have an NHL-standard rink up and running?

Those are the types of concerns that would dictate whether a 34th team is a viable idea and where it could go (assuming, of course, the NHL finds its 33rd in the Lone Star State). -- Shilton

What might the divisions look like if the league adds a 33rd team?
The NHL could look at different scenarios with an odd number of teams.

If there is truly no concern over symmetry, the simplest path forward is slotting the new franchise into an existing division (likely the Central if it's another club in Texas). So the Western Conference would run with 17 teams to the Eastern Conference's 16.

In that case, would there have to be some sort of alteration to the playoff proceedings? And would an uneven number of contenders alter how the NHL puts together its scheduling? Those questions would have to be considered.

That's where another possibility could come into play: restructuring the league into as many as six divisions and spreading out the teams (with four, five or six in each) for balance.

This could leave room for future franchises to join and open the door for the NHL to put in place an entirely fresh playoff realignment, too. But that's a lot of alteration if the NHL intends to add a 34th team in the immediate future. The idea makes sense in the long term regardless of whether Bettman acknowledges the general need for a balance of conferences.

To make a 33-team league work, simply having 17 clubs in the West and 16 in the East is the most sensible path from a practical standpoint. The best suggestion to avoid a sweeping overhaul would be that the NHL at least has a plan in place to go from 33 to 34 franchises in fairly quick succession, however. If the potential to get back to an even number isn't something the league can achieve in a reasonable window, then a broader shakeup -- with realignment and more divisions -- will have to be in play. -- Shilton

What does the NHL board of governors think about expansion in Texas?
We are likely to find out more about the state of NHL expansion at the board of governors meeting in New York on Tuesday.

Deputy commissioner Bill Daly told ESPN last week that he would reach out to the Friedkins for an update, including a temperature check on Austin and Houston as their current focus for NHL expansion. The potential owners informed the league that they'd give both sites a fair shot in their assessment.

What city the Friedkin family chooses has significant ramifications for the board of governors. According to sources, there's a split among the owners on where to expand in Texas. Some of the NHL's most influential owners apparently prefer Houston, especially for its television market. Some of the newer owners are said to prefer Austin.

Whichever group holds the most sway, the ultimate decision comes down to where the NHL's leaders want to go. Bettman and Daly will push for their desired result. It's hard to imagine a scenario in which the board doesn't bend to Bettman's preference.

There's another aspect to the decision worth mentioning: Some owners don't want to expand at all. There are concerns about the player pool being further diluted as well as how expansion would impact the chances of making the cut for a playoff tournament that remains at 16 entrants, sources told ESPN.

Will those concerns manifest as a "no" vote on expansion? Probably not if Bettman is pushing to expand. But they're something to remember if the board is on the fence about a debatable location. -- Wyshynski

What could a TV broadcast deal look like for another Texas-based team?
The NHL will want to be strategic in terms of media potential anywhere it expands. Daly has noted that other possible landing spots Atlanta and Phoenix are the seventh- and 12th-largest TV markets, respectively, in the U.S. Houston is the sixth-largest, while Austin is 34th. When it comes strictly to investigating the options in Texas, it's a serious plus for Houston to hold that sort of reach with the potential for local and national backers to get in on a new franchise.

Looking at a nearby comparable in Dallas shows that the fourth-largest market in the U.S. is home to an exclusive streaming partnership with Amazon Prime for viewers in the region starting in the 2026-27 season. Whether another franchise goes that route or not, it's something to take into account.

There are regional networks and local broadcasts stations in Houston that support the four major pro sports teams already established there. The same sort of attention could be given to an NHL franchise, and hockey could draw a fresh fanbase that opens up a wider range of possible advertisers.

It's hard to say exactly how a TV deal would play out Houston or Austin, but there are multiple options. There isn't a significant precedent for major league sports broadcasting contracts in Austin, though. The only major pro team in the city is Austin FC, whose games are streamed through Apple TV as part of MLS' rights agreement with the platform. The games are then rebroadcast on local television.

The media landscape at large is in flux, especially when it comes to regional broadcasters, so expect the NHL to consider where it can maximize local viewership when it comes to selecting the next expansion spot. -- Shilton

stories.headline: Max vs 100: Meet the drivers racing against Red Bull's Verstappen
stories.summary: Ahead of Max vs 100, here's single driver competing against Max Verstappen in the event streamed live on Disney+.
stories.body:
Four-time Formula 1 world champion Max Verstappen will take on 100 drivers in a unique go-karting event live on ESPN on Disney+ on Sept. 16.

Those competing are a mixture of athletes, content creators, streamers and other personalities from around the world, all with the same goal -- keeping Verstappen behind.

The drivers will be racing around a circuit that has been purpose-built for the occasion.

Here's the confirmed list of drivers taking part so far.

- Max vs 100: F1 superstar Verstappen to race drivers in karting event - live on Disney+

- Max vs 100: When is Verstappen race, how to watch on Disney+, how it works, who's taking part?

- What makes Max Verstappen so good? Career, background and F1 records

Zac Alsop - YouTuber

Alsop has gone viral for his stunts and social experiments. He's been part of several "sneak-in" videos at events including sneaking past security into MMA star Conor McGregor's dressing room on his 30th birthday.

Tyrique Hyde - Streamer

Known for taking part in the reality television show Love Island UK in 2023 and now regularly live-streams on Twitch.

Queen B (Rebecca Evans) - Motorsport creator and presenter

She might be one to watch out for on the track as she started go-karting at eight years old, before doing drag racing aged 14. She has built a career in car culture and has hosted digital content for Top Gear and featured in Red Bull TV original series Drift Queen.

Pieface23 (Jack McDermott) - Content Creator

He's best known for gaming and football and featured on Big Brother UK in 2015. He's now a full-time streamer on Twitch and streams content related to football and video games.

TGFBro (Romell Henry) - YouTube Content Creator
He's amassed over six million subscribers on YouTube since he started in 2012. His channel has videos involving extreme stunts and wild challenges.

Manny (Emmanuel David Brown) - YouTuber

His content is mainly focused on football and he's got two million followers on YouTube. He's also one of the hosts on the podcast 'Family Ties' which he hosts with his brothers.

Dantic (Daniel Moss) - Content Creator and YouTuber

He posts gaming and travel videos which have gone viral online. His videos on YouTube vary between trying every type of water park, trying different tiers of plane seats and gaming in every single train seat on a journey.

Amber Gill - Personality

She has been on several television shows in the UK, but was launched into the spotlight after she won Love Island in 2019. She has since featured on shows such as Celebrity SAS: Who Dares Wins.

Stungpegg (Nieve Petruzziello) - Sports Presenter and Content Creator

She's a popular UK content creator, writer, and presenter with a focus on football content with just under 200,000 followers on Instagram.

Bash The Entertainer (Bachala Mbunzama) - Content Creator and Comedian

He's a Scottish social media influencer and is known for his infectious laugh and famous smile. He's worked with brands such as NFL and Adidas and a video made about Rihanna went viral.

Developer Adam (Adam Powell) - Content Creator
Powell focuses his content on gaming, coding and tech and has also posted several videos on motorsport.

Kalia Lai - Content Creator and Athlete
She's an active runner and does boxing with a focus on general fitness content as well.

James Doyle - Creator

He's from Ireland and posts mainly content related to health and entertainment. He's competed in several HYROX events and has travelled the world including visiting Japan.

Drift Games (David Egan) - Creator

Another driver to potentially watch out for is Egan, who competes in drift racing and also has a YouTube channel that shows you what he gets up to.

GoKartGod - Manufacturer of Electric Go-Karts

The Instagram account is full of content following the next generation of go-karts.

Larry Chen - Photographer

Based in America, he's a car photographer and has over one million followers on Instagram.

Neo Yau (Yau Hawk Sau) - Actor

He's an actor, writer and digital content creator from Hong Kong.

Mike Dokas

His TikTok channel mainly focuses on football and Formula 1 content. He has over 350,000 followers on the platform.

AustrianKiwi (Jonathan Balchin) - Comedian

He makes funny and relatable videos around daily life in Austria.

Nathan Lust - Creator

He's from New Zealand but lives in Australia and has over one million followers on Instagram. His videos are based on comedy including filming behind the scenes on the Avengers and references to Toy Story.

Tettrem (Mateus dos Santos Machado Almeida) - Content creator and co-founder of POV Creators

He's a digital content creator, streamer from Brazil and blew up through viral reaction videos. He has nearly 12 million followers on Instagram.

Mars (Zhang Jing ) - Chinese key opinion leader in extreme sports

From China, his content online features lots of cars and car culture.

Pamkutya (Norbert Osbath) - Content Creator

Osbáth Norbert is a prominent Hungarian content creator, traveler, and author, best known as one-half of PamKutya which he co-founded in 2010.

Roberts Vītols - Content Creator

He's a content creator from Latvia who focuses on cars and culture.

Paky TWC (Patrick Tremolada) - YouTuber

A YouTuber from Italy, he focuses on cool car tricks and has over a million followers on Instagram.

Enis Kirazoğlu - Content Creator

From Türkiye, his content mainly focuses on gaming and he has over 1 million followers on YouTube.

Karol Zdęba - YouTuber

His content is based around adventures with videos including heading to abandoned towns and staying there for several days.

Vale Sulca - Content Creator

Based in the LATAM region, she has half a million followers on Instagram and mainly shares her adventures and lifestyle.

German Rodezel - Content Creator

He's also based in the LATAM region and enjoys making videos and has a passion for music and Formula 1.

Pableke (Pablo Jimenez) - Content Creator

From Chile, his content mainly focuses on motorsport and he has half a million followers on Instagram.

Josh Richards - Creator and Entrepreneur
He's from Canada and is an internet star who rose to fame on TikTok. He's also an entrepreneur and has set up several brands.

Si Hyun Park - Professional Drift Driver

Another one to watch out for, based in South Korea, is a karting driver who focuses on drifting with over one million followers on Instagram.

John-Marc van Wyk - Content Creator

The South African has half a million followers on Instagram and posts lifestyle content.

Dyler - Content Creator

He's a Saudi Arabian artist and content creator with a following of nearly four million people.

Nnnurdaylet - Content Creator

He does a whole heap of different videos and has a huge following of over five million people.

Julia Haller (Julia Alzire Elisabeth Haller) - Content Creator

She posts lifestyle and motorsport content with over 600,000 followers on Instagram.

Wirtual (Øyvind Ludwig Iversen) - Content Creator
He makes videos on Trackmania which is the world's most competitive racing game.

Daniel Ahola - Content Creator

His content features lots of adventures around the world, usually with little to no money.

Gabs Djay - Motorsport Content Creator

She focuses on motorsport news, particularly Formula 1, along with other sports such as football.

Joe Tasker - Content Creator and TV Presenter

He posts comedy videos that most people will be able to relate to and has over 900,000 followers on TikTok.

Bella James - Content Creator

Lots of her content is based around drivers in motorsport, famously interviewing team principals with dry humour.

Juank Perez - Content Creator

Juank is a prominent Latin American sports digital content creator, social media influencer, and digital host for ESPN México.

Fresia Aria - Football Reporter

She's a sports journalist and presenter who has worked for ESPN Netherlands since 2018. Aria covers mainly Dutch football in the Eredivisie.

Nate Saunders - F1 Sports Reporter

Saunders has covered Formula 1 for ESPN since 2014 and has attended races all over the globe, and has interviewed Max Verstappen himself on many occasions.

Jakidale (Jacopo D'Alesio) - YouTuber and Content Creator

He's an Italian YouTuber and creator who makes content on technology, travel and science, with over 600,000 followers on Instagram.

Sporttouchen (Timothé Rangström) - Content Creator
He's a Swedish creator who founded digital sport media company Sporttouchen which is best known for football content aimed at younger audiences.

Bea Eguiraun - Motorsport Content Creator
Eguiraun is a Spanish motorcycle presenter and test rider. She began working professionally in motorsport in 2014 with Dorna Sports, creating social media content and working around MotoGP broadcasts, before going on to present the TV show Locos por las Motos.

TheGrefg - Streamer and Content Creator

He's one of Spain's biggest gaming creators and is particularly known for Fortnite with 12.29 million followers on Twitch and 19.9 million followers on YouTube. In 2021, more than 2.4 million people tuned in to the reveal of his Fortnite skin, which set a Guinness World Record for concurrent viewers on an individual Twitch stream at the time.

Caedrel (Marc Lamont) - Streamer

Lamont is a former professional League of Legends player who moved into League of Legends European Championship (LEC) casting and analytics before becoming a full-time streamer. In 2024, he founded esports organisation Los Ratones and has become one of the biggest personalities in the LoL community.

TheDonato (Donato José Muñoz Calabres) - Streamer and Content Creator

TheDonato is a Venezuelan Red Bull partnered gaming creator who built a huge following through games including Garena Free Fire. He has more than 40 million subscribers on YouTube, with the creator himself crediting his switch to Free Fire as a major turning point in his career.

Helydia (Celia Tansel) - Streamer and Content Creator

Helydia is a French Valorant player and streamer who has built her community through competitive gaming content on Twitch and YouTube. She's also a Red Bull player and regularly takes part in Valorant showmatches and gaming events.

Diogo 'MoveMind' da Silva - Streamer and Content Creator

MoveMind is one of Portugal's best-known streamers and started broadcasting on Twitch as a hobby in 2017. He first broke through while commentating on matches involving professional Portuguese FIFA players and has since made the transition from reporting on esports and virtual FIFA matches to live sports broadcasting of real football games.

Jonathan Amaral - Professional Esports Player

Better known as Jonathan Gaming, Amaral is one of India's leading mobile esports players and is best known for competing in BGMI and PUBG Mobile. In 2026, he launched his own esports organisation, Team Apex Gaming.

RDJavi (Steven Javier Santos del Rosario) - Streamer

RDJavi is a Dominican streamer and gaming YouTuber known widely for his gaming content, particularly GTA V, GTA Roleplay, and automotive vlogs.

TechnoGamerz - Gaming Content Creator

Ujjwal Chaurasia, better known as Techno Gamerz, is one of India's biggest gaming creators and is particularly known for his GTA V content. In 2026, he became the first individual gaming creator in India and all of Asia to pass 50 million subscribers on YouTube.

Amar - Streamer and Entertainer

Amar Al-Naimi, better known as AmarCoDTV, is one of the leading figures in Germany's streaming scene, with content centred around gaming and entertainment. His background includes competitive Call of Duty, while Fortnite has also become a major part of his streaming career.

Nugato - Streamer

Ilija 'Nugato' Ravlić is a Croatian gamer and YouTuber who started creating content in 2013. He became particularly known for Minecraft videos and is now part of Red Bull's gaming roster.

iiTzTimmy (Timothy An) - Streamer

Timothy An, better known as iiTzTimmy, is an American streamer and professional Apex Legends competitor. He's known for marathon gaming challenges, including a Solo Bronze to Predator 34-hour stream that went viral where he went from Rookie to Predator in 126 games.

Qucee (Quentin Correia) - Streamer

Qucee is a Dutch YouTuber, rapper and streamer who is also part of the Supergaande collective. His content has included comedy, street interviews, freestyle rap and live-streaming.

Leticia Bufoni - Professional Skateboarder

Bufoni is a six-time X Games gold medallist, a former world No. 1 and 2015 SLS Super Crown Champion. She holds multiple Guinness World Records and represented Brazil at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics. From go-karting in her youth she's since added motor racing to her résumé and competes in Porsche Cup Brazil, so she could be one to watch on the track.

Sarah Vignot Lezito - Stunt Rider

Sarah Vignot, known professionally as Sarah Lezito is a world-famous French motorcycle stunt rider who began practising her craft as a teenager. Her riding skills have also taken her to Hollywood, where she has performed motorcycle stunt work in major films as a movie stunt double.

Arda Saatçi - Ultra Athlete

Known as 'Cyborg', Saatçi is a German-Turkish extreme endurance athlete and Red Bull Athlete who specialises in extreme endurance challenges. He initially wanted to become a professional footballer, playing for Berliner AK U19 and SV Altlüdersdorf in his youth before injury led him towards endurance sport.

Lethal Shooter (Chris Matthews) - NBA Shooting Coach

Matthews is a former professional basketball player and Red Bull partner who is now one of the sport's most sought-after shooting coaches. Known as 'Lethal Shooter', he's worked with players from both the NBA and WNBA to improve their shooting.

Janja Garnbret - Professional Climber

Garnbret is widely regarded as one of the greatest competition climbers of all time. The Slovenian is a two-time Olympic champion, has won 10 world titles and over 50 World Cup gold medals. In 2026 she recorded her 50th World Cup victory.

Leo Neugebauer - Decathlon World Champion

Neugebauer is a German track and field athlete who won the decathlon world title for Germany in Tokyo in 2025 after previously taking silver at the Paris Olympics. He holds the German national records for both the outdoor decathlon (8,961 points) and the indoor heptathlon as well as taking the men's decathlon title at the Birmingham 2026 European Athletics Championships.

Molly Carlson - Professional Cliff Diver

Carlson is a Canadian high diver, Red Bull cliff diving athlete and a three-time World Championship silver medalist (2022, 2023, and 2024). She's also built a huge online community through her #BraveGang movement to encourage self-love, body positivity, and overcoming fears.

Matt Jones (Matthew Jones) - Red Bull MTB Athlete

Jones is a professional British mountain bike (MTB) freeride and slopestyle athlete. He broke onto the international scene in 2013 and has become known for pushing the limits of the sport with innovative tricks and riding projects.

Billy Bolt - Motorcycle Racer

Bolt should certainly be comfortable with speed as he's a world-renowned, six-time FIM SuperEnduro world champion. The British rider also won the inaugural FIM Hard Enduro World Championship in 2021.

Aidan Heslop - Cliff Diver

Heslop is a British-Welsh high diver who won the men's 27m world title in 2024 at the World Aquatics Championships in Doha. That same year, he was crowned Red Bull Cliff Diving World Series champion after winning four stops during the season.

Pol Tarrés - Enduro Rider

Tarrés is a Spanish trials, hard enduro and rally raid rider who has become known for doing extraordinary things on a Yamaha Ténéré 700. He won the 2024 Morocco Desert Challenge and also set a world record by reaching an altitude of 6,756 metres on a twin-cylinder motorcycle.

Tommo McCluskey - Content Creator

McCluskey, better known online as just Tommo, is a British Formula 1 content creator, presenter and podcaster. He has over 341,000 subscribers on his YouTube channel where he uploads deep dives, quizzes and analysis videos.

Taylor Serage - Content Creator

Taylor Serage is a New Zealand social-media personality and former real-estate agent who has become known for combining fashion, cars, property and lifestyle content on social media. She has over 747,000 followers on Instagram.

Joseph Brophy - TalkSPORT writer

A sports journalist and SEO writer at talkSPORT, specialising in producing digital sports content. He has written extensively across football and other major sporting events.

Supercar Blondie (Niklaus Manuel Hirschi) - CEO and co-founder of Supercar Blondie

Co-founder, along with his wife Alex Hirschi, and CEO of Supercar Blondie, a global automotive media empire. They have over 17 million followers on Instagram and showcase videos of cars, tech and luxury around the world.

Shreeman Legend (Siddhant Praveen Joshi) - Streamer and YouTuber

An Indian gaming content creator and streamer best known for his PUBG Mobile/BGMI content. He became one of India's prominent gaming creators through his energetic gameplay videos and his distinctive blend of Marathi and Hindi commentary.

Shredded Fox (Jan Liška) - YouTuber

A Czech fitness influencer, YouTuber, entrepreneur and former professional online fitness coach. He has spent around a decade in the fitness industry, building a large online following through content about training, nutrition, healthy living and his own fitness journey. He is the only Czech participant in the race.

Molly Marsh - Influencer

A British influencer, musical-theatre performer and television personality, best known for appearing on Love Island series 10 in 2023, where she finished fourth alongside Zachariah Noble.

Mélanie Buffetaud - Content Creator

Buffetaud is a French content creator, filmmaker and parkour athlete. Her content focuses heavily on sport, physical challenges, adventure and pushing the limits. Alongside her partner Charles Poujade, she has built an audience of more than three million subscribers.

Jojo Sim - Content Creator

Jojo Sim is an American social media content creator who makes videos of everything from off-road driving to NASCAR-related content.

MrCarSounds (Greg Gevojanyan) - Content Creator

An American content creator best known for his extraordinary ability to mimic car and engine sounds using his voice. His videos feature everything from supercars and racing cars to trucks and motorcycles, and he has built millions of followers across social media.

ExtraEmily (Emily Xuechun Zhang) - Streamer

Known for her high-energy IRL streams, gaming, challenges and comedic content, Extra Emily is an American Twitch streamer who graduated magna cum laude from Columbia University with a degree in Financial Engineering before pursuing streaming full-time.

Henry Robert Williams (Daily Mail) - Journalist

A British sports presenter and social-media journalist at the Daily Mail, who has said it was his dream to be a sports presenter since the age of 12.

Charles Poujade - Parkour Athlete and Content Creator

Poujade was part of the French team called United that won the 2019 World Chase Tag Championship. He is also a social media creator with a YouTube audience of more than three million.

Austin Sprinz - YouTuber and Content Creator

Austin Sprinz is an American TikTok and YouTube creator from Arizona known for comedy, challenges, experiments and lifestyle content. He has made content across a range of sports including NASCAR, F1, UFC and the Winter Olympics.

Stream Max vs 100 globally on ESPN on Disney+ on Wednesday, Sept. 16. Coverage starts at 5 p.m. BST, before the race begins at 6 p.m.

stories.headline: Citron leads Washington against Chicago after 22-point game
stories.summary: Washington Mystics (24-16, 11-5 Eastern Conference) at Chicago Sky (15-25, 3-13 Eastern Conference)
stories.body:
Washington Mystics (24-16, 11-5 Eastern Conference) at Chicago Sky (15-25, 3-13 Eastern Conference)

Chicago; Thursday, 8 p.m. EDT

LINE: Mystics -3.5; over/under is 167.5

BOTTOM LINE: Washington Mystics plays the Chicago Sky after Sonia Citron scored 22 points in the Mystics' 88-82 loss to the Los Angeles Sparks.

The Sky have gone 3-13 against Eastern Conference teams. Chicago ranks third in the Eastern Conference with 41.7 points per game in the paint led by Kamilla Cardoso averaging 11.1.

The Mystics are 11-5 in Eastern Conference play. Washington ranks sixth in the Eastern Conference with 19.6 assists per game led by Citron averaging 4.3.

Chicago is shooting 44.1% from the field this season, 0.9 percentage points higher than the 43.2% Washington allows to opponents. Washington averages 82.8 points per game, 6.9 fewer points than the 89.7 Chicago allows to opponents.

The teams square off for the second time this season. The Mystics won 90-72 in the last meeting on June 2. Shakira Austin led the Mystics with 17 points, and Sydney Taylor led the Sky with 15 points.

TOP PERFORMERS: Cardoso is averaging 14.8 points, 8.7 rebounds and 1.5 blocks for the Sky. Natasha Cloud is averaging 15.3 points over the last 10 games.

stories.summary: New Inter Miami head coach Cristian "Kily" González said he feels blessed at being given the opportunity to lead the club and coach Lionel Messi, after formerly taking up the role on Tuesday.
stories.body:
FORT LAUDERDALE, Fla. -- New Inter Miami head coach Cristian "Kily" González said he feels blessed at being given the opportunity to lead the club and coach Lionel Messi, after formerly taking up the role on Tuesday.

González has now received the authorization to begin the job after being announced last month as the permanent replacement for interim coach Guillermo Hoyos on a contract through June 2028.

- Source: Colombia targeting U.S. U20 dual national Shaw

- Messi tracker: All goals, assists, key moments for Miami, Argentina in 2026

- Messi scores, but Nashville strikes late to deny Miami win

The job sees him reunite with Messi after the two shared the field for Argentina in two World Cup qualifiers in 2005.

"There are things in football that simply cannot be described in words; they are unique feelings. I feel privileged and blessed to have this opportunity and to share the fantastic relationship I have with Leo," González said in a news conference.

"I adore him, he knows it, and that makes this moment even more special. Being with him and sharing experiences with the incredible players on this squad. Honestly, as a coach, I feel completely fulfilled.

"Of course, this is all wonderful, but now we have to get to work. God willing, we'll start off strong tomorrow and win the championship."

González led his first training session with Inter Miami on Tuesday after landing in Miami from Argentina earlier in the morning. He will be on the sidelines for the team's Campeones Cup match against Liga MX champions Cruz Azul on Wednesday night at Nu Stadium.

Inter Miami reached an agreement with González on Aug. 27, but the coach could not take over for Hoyos until receiving his work permit.

"What were these past few days like? To be honest, they were filled with a lot of anticipation. It had been nearly two and a half weeks and I couldn't be here, but this unique opportunity, something I hadn't even dared to dream of, became a reality," González said.

"We spoke with the club, and they offered me the chance to join the team; I said yes immediately. Being with the players, seeing their willingness to welcome my coaching staff, and watching them train the way they did today honestly, it made me very happy and gave me a huge boost of energy for tomorrow's match."

Miami's opponent in the Campeones Cup was delayed in arriving in Miami for the game and instead of landing in the U.S. on Monday, were unable to fly in until Tuesday.

"Well, more than an odyssey, sometimes accidents like this happen, and you just have to turn the page," said Cruz Azul manager Joel Huiqui. "The team is doing well. We rested very well yesterday, we stayed at a hotel in Mexico, and we're just arriving now. We're calm, obviously aware that tomorrow will be a huge match for us, and we're all focused.

"It goes without saying that [Messis] is a great player, but what matters most to me is that the team realizes what is at stake: not just another trophy, but our consolidation as an institution. Beyond the chance to face a great player, the opportunity to win the title against a team like Inter Miami is about solidifying the work we've been doing and, above all, bringing joy to the fans."

Inter Miami currently sits in second place on the Eastern Conference table with 45 points in 25 games. The team has recorded just one victory in its last nine games.

Inter Miami forward Luis Suárez said he wants to use the game against Cruz Azul to start strong under new leadership.

"When it comes to playing a match like this, it's a final. There is no time to dwell on the past, the only thing that matters is looking ahead to tomorrow," Suárez said. "We've come through a challenging run of games, but now we face the best possible scenario: playing a final and moving forward with a new coach who brings great positive energy, a strong desire to grow and plenty of enthusiasm.

"That attitude is contagious, and we are ready to support him and his coaching staff."

Inter Miami hosts Cruz Azul before returning to Major League Soccer regular season action on Sunday against San Diego.

stories.headline: UFC's Islam Makhachev questions validity of Jon Jones' wins streak
stories.summary: UFC champ Islam Makhachev believes Jon Jones' failed drug tests and issues outside the Octagon invalidate Jones' place among the UFC's all-time streaks for consecutive wins.
stories.body:
Jon Jones and Islam Makhachev, two of the greatest fighters in UFC history, are taking shots at each other this week.

Makhachev (29-1) broke the UFC's official win streak record in August, when he defended his welterweight championship against Ian Machado Garry for his 17th consecutive win. Former middleweight champion Anderson Silva held the previous record of 16. Jones, a former light heavyweight and heavyweight champion, would argue he won 20 bouts in a row from 2010 to 2024, but his streak was interrupted by a no-contest against Daniel Cormier in 2017.

In a recent interview with a Russian news outlet, Makhachev said Jones' no-contest, which was the result of a failed drug test by the United States Anti-Doping Agency, invalidates his win streak.

"I'm not denying that Jon Jones is one of the greatest athletes in history, but he was caught doping twice," Makhachev told Ushatayka. "I think that's why his streak isn't considered valid. Because he went into a fight while on PEDs and won, that's where a new count should have started."

Jonse (28-1) was fined and suspended 15 months for testing positive for extremely trace amounts of steroid metabolites. He initially defeated Cormier in their fight in 2017, before it was later changed to a no-contest.

An independent arbitrator later stated he believed Jones unknowingly ingested the substance and that it was not performance enhancing. Jones has long pointed to that independent finding as validation of his innocence, and did so again Monday in a post directed at Makhachev.

"If you believe USADA for finding a picogram in my system, then you must believe USADA when they say it 'It was not found to be PERFORMANCE ENHANCING or INTENTIONAL,'" Jones wrote on X. "You can't have it both ways. Last I checked, my hand got raised every time I was in the Octagon since any of you can remember. Your own coach said I was 'a gift from God.' Let's not forget you've been KO'd, flatlined, went night night."

Makhachev, whose only loss came by knockout to Adriano Martins in his second UFC fight in 2015, responded to Jones the following day, and hinted at Jones's troubled legal history, both in and out of competition.

"Jon, I'm not trying to diminish your achievements in any way," Makhachev wrote on X. "But your whole life seems to be tied to breaking the rules one way or another, and somehow, you're never the one to be blamed."

stories.headline: Warriors sell out Eden Park in 48 hours amid NRL's crowd woes
stories.summary: Hooker Sam Healey plans to draw inspiration from his rugby league idol to help him handle the pulsating atmosphere of a sold-out Eden Park.
stories.body:
Hooker Sam Healey plans to draw inspiration from his NRL idol to help him handle the pulsating atmosphere of a sold-out Eden Park.

The NRL announced that general-public tickets for Sunday's do-or-die semi-final between the Warriors and Newcastle in Auckland had sold out in less than 48 hours.

It comes after New Zealand were forced to relocate from their traditional home ground for the clash because Eden Park hosts about 25,000 more spectators than Go Media Stadium.

The 50,000-seat venue being full comes after the league was criticised over poor crowd numbers in the first week of finals, although the Warriors had a mostly sold-out attendance for their 26-16 loss to the Dolphins.

Regardless, it's the club's first clash at Eden Park since 2014, and will be a mammoth moment for New Zealand rugby league as the Warriors look to keep alive their hopes of a first premiership.

Healey is yet to play at the venue, but will be wanting to produce similar heroics to his idol Kevin Locke, who made a courageous try-saving tackle on Sydney Roosters centre Michael Jennings at the Fortress in 2013.

"I have played league since I was five or six or something like that, so I always loved the game," Healey said.

"I actually saw him (Locke) in the sheds the other day, and I said to my mum, 'Do you remember when he was my favourite player'. She just started laughing.

"He used to be my lock-screen on my phone ... I just said g'day."

Warriors back-rower Jacob Laban has only played once at the country's biggest sporting stadium.

"It was Kiwi A's versus Tonga A's, I think it was two, three years ago," he said.

"(After) New Zealand played Samoa (in the Pacific Championships) ... it was a pretty cool, good atmosphere.

"Obviously it (the crowd) is a little bit further (away) than Mt Smart, but it's not too bad. When you score a try, you can walk up to the fans over there, so it's still pretty close."

Laban won't be intimidated by the history of Eden Park, although the club has won only one of its six games at the venue.

The blond second-rower is intent on not just helping the Warriors set up a preliminary final against Penrith, but also on making his childhood self proud.

"I knew I wanted to play for the Warriors when I first heard about rugby league," Laban said.

"They came to Wellington. I don't know what year it was, but I still have this photo of me where I had half a Warriors face painted on and a Warriors T-shirt.

"I knew I wanted to play for the Warriors since I was young."

stories.headline: Brooklyn Nets offseason recap, early 2026-27 season preview
stories.summary: Can Brooklyn finally build toward contention? We're recapping the offseason and taking an early look at 2026-27.
stories.body:
The Brooklyn Nets had another troubling season in 2025-26, finishing near the bottom of the league with a 20-62 record -- their third worst in franchise history. Plus, to add insult to injury, their crosstown rivals, the New York Knicks, celebrated with the city after winning their first NBA championship in 53 years.

However, the Nets are looking toward the future, starting with the development of their young core after GM Sean Marks used his stockpile of a historic five first-round picks in 2025 to nab Egor Demin, Nolan Traore, Drake Powell, Ben Saraf and Danny Wolf, and added three more from this year's deep draft class.

Their biggest offseason acquisition was trading for Julius Randle, who will be joining Michael Porter Jr., Moritz Wagner and Keon Ellis to lead this young core under third-year coach Jordi Fernandez.

But will this all be enough for the Nets to start building toward contention in an increasingly competitive Eastern Conference?

ESPN's staff of experts is looking back at the offseason and taking an early look at the 2026-27 season, with 30 previews -- one for every team -- rolling out each weekday through Friday. We're answering the biggest looming questions, evaluating X factors and much more.

Quick links:

Roster | Depth chart | Transactions

More Nets coverage | More NBA

Offseason at a glance
Key additions: F Julius Randle, G Mikel Brown Jr., G Keon Ellis

Key subtractions: C Nic Claxton

Key retentions: C Day'Ron Sharpe, F Josh Minott

Once commissioner Adam Silver responded to last season's shameless tankathon by nearly a third of the league's teams by implementing a draft lottery reform, the Nets could no longer slow-play their rebuild by hoping for ping-pong luck. Getting Randle back to New York, but this time across town from his former team, and one he watched win an NBA championship without him, was a big move for the Nets. Plus, drafting a promising point guard, Brown at No. 6, in this year's draft adds to a glut of guards on the roster, but the Nets were in serious need of a talent upgrade across the board. Even with the addition of Randle, who's due to make $33.3 million this season, the Nets are still well below the salary cap, meaning they can take in plenty of money in deals should the opportunity present itself. -- Vincent Goodwill

Zach Kram's offseason grade: B-

The Nets mostly used their cap space on small-scale contracts: Minott, Ellis, Wagner and Sharpe -- the last of those quietly one of the best deals of the offseason. Their largest outlay came from trading Claxton in a deal that brought back former All-NBA forward Randle, which should improve the team next season -- because of Randle's availability and floor-raising talent -- but doesn't do much to aid the Nets' murky longer-term outlook. Brooklyn doesn't control its 2027 first-round pick, with Houston holding swap rights. -- Kram

What we learned this offseason
From Ben Golliver's offseason lessons piece: The Nets are still buying time.

The Houston Rockets own the right to swap 2027 first-round picks with the Nets, so Brooklyn entered the summer with motivation to take a big swing. If the Nets' ongoing youth movement was unlikely to deliver a lottery pick next June, why not dangle some of their future draft assets in trades that could help them be more competitive after a dismal 20-win campaign?

Although Brooklyn acquired Randle in a deal with the Minnesota Timberwolves, the 31-year-old forward isn't talented enough to carry a contender or young enough to shepherd the Nets' next era. Randle should help Brooklyn make progress in the standings, but plugging him in as a stopgap doesn't qualify as a long-term plan.

Nets general manager Sean Marks has preached the importance of strategic "flexibility," and for now that means waiting on the development of lottery picks Demin and Brown. Demin's strong showing at summer league hinted that the Russian guard could be headed for a second-year breakout that would bring much-needed clarity to the wayward Nets. -- Golliver

The big question: Can the Nets form an identity against the backdrop of Knicks mania?
It would be easy to say the Nets aren't paying attention to what's happening in Manhattan, but nobody would believe that. For years, the Nets' biggest advantage was that the Knicks hadn't found their way to contention, which is now no longer the case. Porter is in the last year of his deal and was productive before being shut down in the last month of the season as the Nets angled for better draft positioning. The Nets held on to each of their first-round picks from 2025, throwing them into the deep end, and hopefully those swings will start showing promise starting this season. Adding Randle will help at least ease any unwanted attention, as he'll field the questions and pressure of playing for New York's second-thought team. That group needs an innings eater, especially as Brown comes into his own, and Randle, if nothing else, will take up plenty of minutes and shots as the Nets hope to gain an identity before beginning to think of developing a foothold in New York. -- Goodwill

Basketball Power Index rank: No. 29
Here are the predicted net points per 100 possessions for the Nets' top seven players for the 2026-27 season:

Randle's decline in the second half of last season was plain to see. He posted plus-2.2 net points per 100 possessions in the first half of the season, just 0.0 in the second half, along with 10 negative games out of 13 in the playoffs. Such a sudden drop-off was probably either due to injury or the situation in Minnesota demotivating him. However, he should be solid and make the Nets a bit more competitive this season. -- Dean Oliver

Read about how net points works here.

Biggest X factor this season
G Nolan Traore, G Drake Powell, G Ben Saraf and F Danny Wolf

Demin, the No. 8 pick in the 2024 draft, looked like a solid NBA player in his rookie season before injury cut it short, and he took even greater strides in a summer league cameo. But the other four members of Brooklyn's large class of 2024 first-round picks offer much more uncertain futures.

The Nets probably knew they weren't going to go a perfect five-for-five with their picks that year, particularly because Demin was the only lottery selection. But it would sure be nice if at least one or two others flashed greater potential in their sophomore seasons, so the Nets can pencil them with greater confidence into their long-term plans. -- Kram

Fantasy insight from our expert
Fantasy insight ahead of the season: Pay close attention to the Nets' young starting backcourt of rookie No. 5 pick Brown and last season's No. 8 overall selection Demin. Demin battled injury for much of his rookie campaign and averaged roughly 10/3/3 in 52 games, but he showed flashes of all-around upside and averaged 21.0 PPG, 4.3 APG and 2.3 SPG in 25.3 MPG in Las Vegas summer league. Brown, meanwhile, showed flashes of his own this summer while averaging 16.7 PPG and 4.0 APG in 22.5 MPG in summer league. The rebuilding Nets should give their backcourt of the future plenty of minutes and opportunities to produce fantasy-worthy stats this season. -- Andre Snellings

stories.headline: What New York Mets learned in 2026
stories.summary: Despite an astronomical payroll, the Mets won't be playing in October ... again. Time to pick up the pieces for 2027.
stories.body:
The New York Mets have 11 games remaining in another disappointing season that began with World Series aspirations and ended with them playing the role of pesky spoiler against several postseason contenders down the stretch.

And that is the duality of the Mets' season: a colossal letdown from a roster with the second-highest payroll in the majors, but enough silver lining for optimists to generate excitement for 2027. The Mets are 21-16 since trading eight big leaguers in the weeks leading into the Aug. 3 deadline. They've played 13 teams during that stretch, eight of them currently sitting in a playoff spot and two others just four games under .500 combined. They've been a good baseball team for six weeks.

"It just shows what guys can do collectively together when they're on the field, when they're healthy," Mets interim manager Andy Green said. "It gives us a glimpse of what we're capable of, living up to that throughout the course of the season. It doesn't put us starting the season next year 5-0 or anything like that. It does no good in that regard. But it does breed confidence and breathe life into a group that believes in themselves."

That belief extends to a front office led by president of baseball operations David Stearns and into owner Steve Cohen's suite. The Mets expect to contend in 2027. The pressure is on from a frustrated fanbase that expressed its feelings loud and clear Monday and Tuesday with chants calling for Stearns' firing while celebrating Pete Alonso's return to Queens with the Baltimore Orioles.

The awkwardness of this week's events aside -- fans at Citi Field openly rooted for Alonso, giving him a curtain call after he clubbed his 300th career home run against their team, which bothered Mets players -- it's been a positive stretch for New York. On top of ending the season on a high note, here are some lessons they learned from an unsatisfying 2026.

Francisco Lindor and Juan Soto can coexist
The future of the Mets begins with their franchise pillars. The organization reshaped its core last winter by not re-signing Alonso and trading Brandon Nimmo and Jeff McNeil, opting to build the roster around Soto and Lindor, the team's highest-paid players.

That choice was made despite the stars' palpable tension throughout their first season together in 2025. The relationship remained icy until thawing this summer with help from starter Freddy Peralta, who initiated a meeting between the two players in June.

Since then, according to sources, the relationship between the two All-Stars has greatly improved. Peralta's performance on the mound was a huge disappointment before he was sent to the Tampa Bay Rays at the trade deadline, but his leadership could have a significant impact on the franchise's future.

Injuries to both players factored into the Mets' disappointing 2026 campaign. Lindor and Soto have played in just 44 games together this season. The Mets are 21-23 with both of them in the lineup, 48-59 without both in there.

The Mets' success in 2027 starts with them.

The outfield is set 'for many years'
The Mets might have stumbled into their most encouraging development of the 2026 season.

If the offseason went as the Mets had hoped, they would have signed Kyle Tucker. If they had added Tucker and gone on to acquire Luis Robert Jr. as they did, Carson Benge would not have made the Opening Day roster. But Tucker chose to sign with the Los Angeles Dodgers -- and has been underwhelming, to say the least -- and the Mets pivoted to signing Bo Bichette. That left a corner outfield spot open for Benge on Opening Day.

Six weeks later, with Robert on the injured list, A.J. Ewing was called up. After beginning the season in Double-A, Ewing impressed right off the bat and became a big-league regular.

The two rookies and Soto -- with Nick Morabito, another rookie, spelling Soto in left field -- should give the Mets a formidable outfield for years to come.

After struggling to handle velocity over the first month, the 23-year-old Benge adjusted and gleaming results followed. Benge slashed .136/.219/.197 with one home run in his first 21 games. Since then, he's slashing .291/.352/.445 with 17 home runs in 124 games as he's settled into his role as the everyday right fielder. Defensively, the former college pitcher boasts one of the best outfield arms in the majors and is tied for third in MLB with 10 outfield assists.

Ewing has been an elite center fielder -- his 10 defensive runs saved in just 109 games ranks 11th among all outfielders. He's been streakier at the plate than Benge, batting .274 with a .771 OPS in his first 63 games and .178 with a .474 OPS in his next 35 contests. He's now batting .400 with a 1.132 OPS over his past 11 games.

"I am encouraged by what we've seen," Stearns said. "We've seen continued progression from a lot of players who are going to be here next year and for many years beyond. And that is very encouraging for me."

'You can never have too much starting pitching'

Nolan McLean will likely finish in the top three in NL Rookie of the Year voting, while Christian Scott and Zac Thornton have made strong cases for inclusion in next year's rotation. Veteran lefty Sean Manaea, who will be in the final year of his deal, and right-hander Jonah Tong, who had his best start as a big leaguer Monday against the Orioles, are also in the mix. But the Mets will need to address the rotation again this offseason and there's one obvious target.

Tarik Skubal, according to ESPN's Jeff Passan, could sign for more than $400 million this offseason. Only a few teams can swim in those deep waters. The Mets are one of them. Stearns, however, has a history of not pursuing elite free agent starters in their early 30s and Skubal turns 30 in November. Yes, Stearns went hard after Yoshinobu Yamamoto, but he was 25 when he came over from Japan. Skubal is five years older.

The Mets' formula produced an unexpected trip to the NLCS in 2024, but starting pitching has been a problem over the past two disappointing seasons.

"I think there are a number of lessons there," Stearns said. "You can never have too much starting pitching. You have to provide yourself avenues on your roster to give other players a chance when you're not getting the performance expected. And I think in both of those areas, through the first couple of months, we came up short."

Last winter, Stearns opted to trade two top prospects for Peralta, who was coming off a career All-Star season. Notably, he was due to make just $8 million in 2026. That move backfired. Maybe this is the offseason and Skubal, a two-time Cy Young Award winner, is the pitcher who bucks the trend.

Kodai Senga's bullpen tryout was a success
The bullpen was another one of the few strengths this season. The Mets ranked ninth in the majors in bullpen ERA entering Tuesday. That's despite trading four relievers at the deadline and closer Devin Williams landing on the injured list less than a week later.

Since the deadline, the Mets rank 15th in bullpen ERA, with Senga taking over the closer role. Senga surrendered the home run to Alonso to blow his first save Tuesday, but he has shined in the ninth inning otherwise, with seven saves behind a fastball that touches 100 mph and his trademark forkball. Whether Senga is in the bullpen in 2027 is unclear. As we mentioned, the Mets could use more starting pitching depth.

But Senga, who will make $15 million in the final guaranteed year of his contract, has not been reliable as a starter since the middle of last season.

"It's fun to see," Green said. "I think his investment in that role, even though he views himself as a starter, I think he prefers to start, but his investment in that role, and the way he embraced that role, I think is a great example for his teammates, for the organization as a whole. He's done a great job. Where is that going forward next year is still to be determined, but it's been great to see. He's had some really good stuff at times coming out of the 'pen."

They still need to find a manager
Also still be determined: The Mets' manager next season.

Green was the organization's vice president of player development before going back into the dugout for his second stint as manager. It has gone much better than his first -- he went 274-366 in nearly four seasons at the helm with the San Diego Padres -- with a 35-35 record through Tuesday.

While Green has earned praise for his work since replacing Carlos Mendoza in late June, he has insisted that he plans on returning to the front office after the season. Whether that means he returns to his player development role is unclear.

"I think Andy's done a very good job in the dugout," Stearns said. "Again, I think we will get to the point where I'll more fully describe what we're seeking in our next manager."

The list of possible candidates includes former Mets outfielder Carlos Beltrán, former Boston Red Sox manager Alex Cora, former Minnesota Twins manager Rocco Baldelli, former Chicago Cubs manager David Ross and current Houston Astros manager Joe Espada, who is in the last year of his contract.

There is such a thing as doing too much in the offseason
Last offseason, the Mets overhauled Mendoza's coaching staff before dramatically changing the roster. Last month, Cohen acknowledged that the club "might've taken too much risk" with so many wholesale changes. The risk included acquiring Polanco and Robert, talented veterans with extensive injury histories that resurfaced this season.

"I think we have to evaluate how we're assessing injury risk as it relates to the entirety of our roster," Stearns said earlier this season. "There are definitely some guys ... who have had previous injury history. We've also had some players who have spent prolonged periods on the injured list this year who have been among the most durable players in all of baseball. So we've kind of been hit by all sides of it.

"But, yeah, I think whenever you bring in a player with injury history, we are aware there's heightened injury risk. In many cases, we thought we were insulated by that risk in certain areas of our roster with other players and we haven't been."

A new manager could mean another coaching staff makeover -- managers often want to bring in their own people -- but another round of sweeping roster changes isn't likely this winter.

stories.headline: Aleksander Barkov appreciating Panthers return after lost season
stories.summary: In the mind of Panthers captain Aleksander Barkov, the difficult part of his comeback is already over.
stories.body:
FORT LAUDERDALE, Fla. -- In the mind of Florida Panthers captain Aleksander Barkov, the difficult part of his comeback is already over.

It happened in May, in a far-from-filled Swedish arena, when Barkov suited up for Finland in an exhibition against Switzerland for his first game since shredding his right knee in the Panthers' first training camp practice 7½ months earlier. On one of his first shifts, he tumbled to the ice.

Nothing bad happened.

"Very good news," Barkov said.

That was it. That was all it took for Barkov to realize his surgically repaired knee was good, that he could play without fear or concern. A few weeks later, he hoisted the trophy when Finland won the IIHF world championship.

Now he is home in Florida, set for the start of training camp and ready to lead a team that, even after missing the playoffs last season, has been set by most sportsbooks as the favorite to win what would be its third Stanley Cup in a four-year span.

"Don't take anything for granted," Barkov said, when asked what he learned from not being able to play for Florida last season. "You just have to enjoy every single chance you get to play hockey, to be with your teammates, to go to every single practice, every single game. You've got to be excited about that."

The Panthers, who were holding media day on Wednesday in advance of Thursday's first practice of camp, have plenty of reasons to be excited. Many core players from the runs to the Cup titles in 2024 and 2025 are back, names like Barkov, Matthew Tkachuk, Sam Reinhart, Sam Bennett, Aaron Ekblad, Carter Verhaeghe, Gustav Forsling, Brad Marchand, Anton Lundell, Dmitry Kulikov and Niko Mikkola.

Brady Tkachuk, Matthew's brother, has been added to the mix, and Florida even brought Radko Gudas -- a fan favorite from his first stint with the Panthers -- back to help shore up the defense. In net, with Sergei Bobrovsky gone to Toronto, Florida is turning the goaltender job over to Jacob Markstrom.

"Every single guy who has come in, they look so determined to be their best and to show their best," Barkov said. "But they also know that we're all in this together. Every single person is important, and every single has their own abilities to lead in their own way. We have many of those guys, so that's the best part of this. No one's here by themselves. Everyone can be just whatever they are."

That didn't happen last season. Injuries gutted the Panthers, starting with Barkov.

He got hurt about 20 minutes into the first practice of training camp, tearing the ACL and MCL in his right knee on Sept. 25, 2025. He had surgery a day later and was skating within a few months, but by the time he was ready to seriously consider returning to game action, Florida was out of playoff contention.

It wasn't entirely a lost season for Barkov. He missed the chance to serve as Finland's captain at the Milan Cortina Olympics but played for his country at the IIHF world championships in the spring and got to hoist the trophy when Finland beat host Switzerland 1-0 in the gold medal game.

Florida's career leader in goals and assists is raring to go with the Panthers once again.

"We all know camp is always going to be hard, no matter what. It's going to be hard physically and mentally," Barkov said. "We're all kind of ready for that test."

stories.headline: Max vs 100 explained: Rules, drivers, shortcuts and how Verstappen can win
stories.summary: Everything you need to know ahead of Max v 100 at Silverstone, as Max Verstappen takes on a unique new challenge.
stories.body:
In one of the most unique challenges ever faced by a Formula 1 driver, Max Verstappen is taking to Silverstone on Wednesday, where he will try to overtake 100 drivers in just 30 laps.

Verstappen first sat in a kart at the age of four and was taking part in competition by the age of seven -- but has been in Formula 1 for the past 11 years.

He's set to roll back the years and test his go-karting pedigree once more against drivers from the world of social media, TV and sport.

Here's everything you need to know about Max vs 100.

- Max vs 100: Meet the drivers racing against Red Bull's Verstappen

- Max vs 100: F1 drivers predict how Verstappen will fare racing 100 drivers

- How Verstappen's karting years prepared him for an all-new test

What is Max vs 100?
Max vs 100 is a one-off go-kart race organised by Red Bull, which sees four-time Formula 1 world champion Max Verstappen attempt to beat 100 amateur drivers from around the world at Silverstone.

What does Verstappen have to do to win?
Verstappen will start from the back of the grid, with all 100 competitors ahead of him. He will have 30 laps to overtake all of them in order to win.

When a kart is overtaken by Verstappen, they are out, meaning Verstappen could win before the 30 laps are complete.

What is the 'fast lap' and how do the shortcuts work?
Anyone attempting to hold off one of the greatest Formula 1 drivers of all time will need a little bit of help, and Max vs 100 competitors will have access to a 'fast lap' once during the race.

Drivers will be able to use their 'fast lap' at any time in the first 15 laps of the race, which will enable to them to take a shortcut on the track and gain some ground back on Verstappen when he begins to close in.

However, Verstappen has one available of his own to gain time -- but he cannot use it until the last 15 laps.

How does qualifying work?
The grid order will be determined by one flying lap around the specially-designed course at Silverstone -- with just a single attempt available. Much like in Formula 1, the grid order will be determined by lap times.

Are all the karts the same?
Every kart is identical. The complete weight, including driver and kit, must reach 85kg, meaning ballast will be added to karts which do not reach the total, levelling out the field.

Who are the 100 drivers facing Verstappen?
Among the drivers taking on Verstappen are personalities from TV, social media, and sport, though no professional racing drivers are included.

The list includes streamers Pieface, Caedrel and TheDonato, ultrarunner Arda Saatçi, basketball shooting phenomenon Chris "Lethal Shooter" Matthews, and 2019 Love Island winner Amber Gill.

Verstappen will be able to communicate with the field directly during the race, offering an insight into his racing brain.

How difficult will Max vs 100 be?
Verstappen's challenge in this race will not be in terms of raw pace or lap times, where he is certain to be a cut above the rest.

The issues will come in the form of traffic -- with so many karts ahead of him and some very likely to be lapped -- and time management, as Verstappen will need to calculate where and when he is to attempt passes.

A few of the field, while not professional, are karting influencers who know how to get round a track, and will want to make the most of their opportunity to defend against a Formula 1 icon.

When and how do I watch it?
Max vs 100 is taking place on Sept. 16, and will be shown live globally on ESPN on Disney+.

In the U.S., Max v 100 will also air on the ESPN App for Unlimited subscribers before a delayed ESPN2 broadcast later that day.

The race itself will start at 6 p.m., with the live stream beginning one hour before.

Comedian Mo Gilligan will front the coverage, which is set to include drone footage and live race data.

Stream Max vs 100 globally on ESPN on Disney+ on Wednesday, Sept. 16. Coverage starts at 5 p.m. BST, before the race begins at 6 p.m.

stories.headline: Connecticut faces Atlanta after Edwards' 26-point showing
stories.summary: Connecticut Sun (10-30, 3-14 Eastern Conference) at Atlanta Dream (26-14, 11-5 Eastern Conference)
stories.body:
Connecticut Sun (10-30, 3-14 Eastern Conference) at Atlanta Dream (26-14, 11-5 Eastern Conference)

College Park, Georgia; Thursday, 7:30 p.m. EDT

LINE: Dream -14.5; over/under is 169.5

BOTTOM LINE: Connecticut Sun visits the Atlanta Dream after Aaliyah Edwards scored 26 points in the Sun's 97-71 loss to the Dallas Wings.

The Dream are 11-5 in conference games. Atlanta ranks second in the Eastern Conference with 21.1 assists per game led by Jordin Canada averaging 7.4.

The Sun are 3-14 in Eastern Conference play. Connecticut ranks third in the WNBA with 9.2 offensive rebounds per game led by Brittney Griner averaging 1.9.

Atlanta averages 90.8 points per game, 3.0 more points than the 87.8 Connecticut gives up. Connecticut averages 79.0 points per game, 6.7 fewer points than the 85.7 Atlanta allows to opponents.

The teams square off for the third time this season. In the last meeting on Aug. 13 the Dream won 104-69 led by 29 points from Rhyne Howard, while Edwards scored 15 points for the Sun.

TOP PERFORMERS: Howard is averaging 18.3 points, 3.6 assists and 2.3 steals for the Dream. Allisha Gray is averaging 19.3 points over the last 10 games.

Olivia Nelson-Ododa is averaging 10 points and 5.9 rebounds for the Sun. Edwards is averaging 10.1 points and 3.8 rebounds while shooting 55.9% over the last 10 games.

LAST 10 GAMES: Dream: 7-3, averaging 94.6 points, 38.1 rebounds, 22.0 assists, 8.0 steals and 4.1 blocks per game while shooting 44.1% from the field. Their opponents have averaged 85.0 points per game.

Sun: 3-7, averaging 76.3 points, 31.3 rebounds, 18.4 assists, 7.5 steals and 4.0 blocks per game while shooting 39.5% from the field. Their opponents have averaged 89.1 points.

INJURIES: Dream: Brionna Jones: out (leg).

Sun: Brittney Griner: day to day (knee), Kennedy Burke: out for season (shoulder), Olivia Nelson-Ododa: day to day (knee).
